## TL;DR

Fixed the check-gate drift classifier so source edits in the commit history invalidate a running check even if a later commit reverts them. This resolves both review findings: endpoint diffs can no longer hide transient source changes, and a non-empty source diff fails closed when inspected history cannot account for it. Bookkeeping-only changes remain allowed. Updated the regression test and user-facing and engineering documentation. The required scoped check passed after formatting the classifier.

## Work and rationale

The review identified two related gaps in `checkGateHeadDriftAllowed`. First, its early return treated the final tree as the whole story: if a source edit was committed and reverted during a check, the endpoint diff was empty and the check was accepted. That is unsafe because validation can observe an intermediate source tree. Second, the helper could return clean when it found a net source diff but could not associate that diff with any inspected commit.

I changed the classifier to retain the endpoint diff as a fallback and inspect the commits on the first-parent path between the checked HEAD and the later HEAD. Source paths touched by those commits are collected with their commit subjects. A source commit followed by a revert therefore remains a rejection and its message explains both subjects and the affected path. The existing merge handling remains important: commits already in the checked tree are not treated as new drift, and merge results are compared with the tree that was actually checked. Bookkeeping paths under the configured work and cache roots continue to be ignored.

When Git cannot enumerate the history or compute paths for an intervening commit, the result now fails closed, including cases where the endpoint diff is empty. When endpoint source paths remain unexplained by the inspected commits, they also invalidate the check and are named in the refusal. This keeps a real final source delta from being silently accepted because history inspection was incomplete.

The regression test that previously encoded acceptance of a change followed by a revert now requires rejection and checks for both commit subjects and `src/app.ts`. The focused bookkeeping test suite passed. I also revised `docs/check-run-history.md` and `user-docs/check.md` to describe intermediate-commit inspection, fail-closed behavior, and the source drift refusal accurately.

## Approaches tried

The original implementation established drift from the net tree difference, then used commit history only to explain that net change. That approach kept bookkeeping-only commits inexpensive and correctly caught ordinary source changes, but it could not detect a source change that had been reverted before validation ended. It also made the history explanation secondary to an endpoint result that can be empty.

I replaced that shortcut with an inspection of each commit in the gate interval while retaining the endpoint comparison as a safety net. I considered preserving the endpoint-only acceptance as an acknowledged limitation because earlier task notes had described that behavior. The latest review explicitly called it a bug: a running check may have observed the intermediate tree. I followed that finding and corrected both the implementation and docs instead of retaining the old limitation.

## Challenges and blockers

The first required scoped check completed remote validation successfully, including all selected tests, but its local formatting guard found one formatting issue in the classifier. I ran the repository formatter, which changed only that classifier line, and reran the complete required check.

Two remote attempts on `thinkpad` were detected by RepoOS as hung and discarded. RepoOS retried on another configured runner, where the complete remote build and tests passed. No runner process was stopped manually. The second check then completed all local guards, including formatting, lint, build, rendered contrast, UI smoke, and the user documentation build. The documentation generator emitted its existing warning about a sidebar anchor without a matching page heading; the build and link checks passed.

## Key learnings

A clean endpoint diff does not prove a check saw an unchanged source tree: the commit sequence matters when content can be changed and reverted during the run. Drift classification should use commit history to detect any check-relevant source touch, and should use the endpoint diff to make unexplained net changes fail closed. Bookkeeping tolerance should remain path-based so task records and cache data can move without pretending source history is harmless.

For this change, the targeted regression suite was useful for fast feedback, but the prescribed scoped RepoOS check provided the final evidence: remote build and tests, followed by local format, lint, build, style guards, rendered contrast, smoke test, and docs build. The first attempt also confirmed that a formatter failure must be corrected and the entire gate rerun; a successful remote test phase alone is not a green check.
